body: The only light in 412 is the one inside the RAZR. Jack is holding it open over his face at the end of an arm that went to sleep around six, and past it, over Theo’s desk, the window is starting to have things in it: the eucalyptus along the Lagoon first, black on a lesser black, then the sky letting itself in behind the trees a shade at a time. He got in from the Saturday close at twenty past one and slept till five. Since five he has been on his back on his own bed with the phone open to SKYE (MISFIT), in her capitals.
In the lot she switched the guessing off so she could spell her own name. At five he switched it back on, because one letter at a time would take him till Thanksgiving.
*hi its jack.* Deleted. She typed herself into this phone and called herself from it. She knows who it is.
*about last night* — that’s how you start a confession, or a country song, and he doesn’t want to be in either one. Deleted.

*thanks for the* — and then the 5, the 4, the 7, the 7. The RAZR, guessing, offers him a word. He presses down on the little silver pad and it offers him the other word that lives on the same four keys. He shuts the phone on both of them like it bit him, and lies there with it closed on his breastbone.

When he opens it again he types *the grandmother*, and that one he keeps. He knows what he wants to say: she was wrong. He has known it since the den, since LIAR four times down a margin in Sharpie, and he has the argument — he had it Friday, he had it again last night at the Anchor sink with his arms in the rinse water — and it’s a good argument, and it runs about four pages. Jack Costigan, who will argue with anybody about anything at two in the morning for the pleasure of it, cannot get being right into a hundred and sixty characters. Every word he takes out is a word he needs. He takes them out anyway. *the grandmother* sits on the little screen with the cursor blinking after it, waiting on the rest.
At twenty to seven the door opens and Theo comes in.

His khakis are wet to the shin, and above the wet they’re crusted with sand, and his loafers have gone dark with the sea. He’s carrying a gas-station coffee in a paper cup with the lid on. His hair is perfect.
“You’re up,” Theo says.
“You’re out.”
Theo takes the lid off the coffee, blows across it, and puts the lid back on. “I run now.”
His eyes go to the phone open in Jack’s hand. Jack shuts it.

Theo says nothing, at volume. He sets the coffee on the desk by the MacBook, steps out of the loafers where he stands, and lies down on his bed with his sandy ankles crossed and his hands folded on his chest.

The coffee steams on the desk. The window is light enough to read by now. After a minute Jack turns on his side toward the wall and opens the RAZR again under the edge of the blanket, where the light won’t carry to Theo’s side of the room, and the cursor is still blinking after *the grandmother*.

body.text: 10–0 or bust. Sully’s at ten. Bring your Browns face. —L.

body: Sully’s has three televisions going and two that matter. The big screen over the bar has the Saints in Tampa. The tube in the corner has the Browns in Detroit, and under it, on his stool at the end of the bar, is Dale Wisniewski in the Barry Sanders jersey with a stack of quarters by his glass. His Lions went oh and sixteen last year. He has been there since they unlocked the door. The third set has the Steelers in Kansas City, and nobody at Sully’s has an opinion about it but the bartender.

Lena has the chair under the bell, in black and gold, with the rope tied off to its cleat at her elbow and a Kleenex up her sleeve. Friday’s cold has gone down into her chest and left her a voice like a gravel road. Julian has pulled a stool up beside her chair, in a cardigan, learning: he watches the snap, and then he watches Lena to find out whether it was good.

“Laney gave me your message,” she tells Jack when he sits down. “I was ahead of you. I ate it cold, out of the quart, standing at the sill at six in the morning.” She points the Kleenex at him. “Don’t you dare tell Gloria.”

Laney is in sunglasses at ten in the morning and has said good morning to nobody. She’s looking under the table, at Jack’s boots. Every time he shifts his feet a little more of Ellery Beach comes out of the welts onto Sully’s floorboards.
“Fireman,” Laney says, “why is there a *beach* in your boots?”
Then the Saints break the huddle, and she turns back to the screen before he has to have an answer.

Kevin drove. He keeps score on a bar napkin with a golf pencil, both games in two neat columns. Theo is asleep in 412. On the fourth chair, where Becca sat last week with her celery, there’s Laney’s purse.

body.text: “Where’s her saint?” Dale asks the bartender, looking along the bar for St. Jude. Lena answers for him, in the gravel. “He has limits, Dale.”

body: It’s seven all after a quarter, and Lena sits forward on the chair with both fists on her knees. Then the Saints score, and score again, and keep scoring — thirty-one points in a row — and every time, the owner unties the rope and Lena stands up on the rung and rings it and does a WHO DAT that comes out mostly gravel.

Between series the RAZR is open under the table, below the edge, where Jack writes something and takes it back out. *you had her backwards* — true, and no way to say good morning to anybody. Out. *re: the ditch* — it reads like a work order from Lordstown. Out.
Lena catches him at it once. “Who’re you texting?”
“No one.”
She looks at him over the Kleenex. Then Brees is throwing again, and she lets him have it.

In the corner, meanwhile, Brady Quinn is throwing touchdown passes, which a Browns quarterback isn’t supposed to be able to do. Jack, who buried Quinn in this same bar on Monday, with full honors, starts exhuming him a drive at a time. The second touchdown he calls a clerical error. The third, a sign. Lena, between Saints scores, tells him the Saints once went three and thirteen in a city that wasn’t theirs and she watched every snap, and asks whether he’d like a tissue for his hope.
Kevin, who doesn’t follow the Browns, leans across with the golf pencil. “Is this good? Your face says it’s bad.”
“It’s good,” Jack says. “That’s why my face says it’s bad.”
Quinn throws a fourth, and Jack, who was raised to know better, lets himself hope. The Browns lose on the last play of the game, thirty-eight to thirty-seven.

Dale comes off his stool with both arms over his head. Then he turns around and sees Jack’s face, and he brings his arms down and sits back on the stool and lifts a finger to the bartender, and a root beer comes sliding down the bar.
“Told you,” Dale says. “A tragedy either way.” He raises his own glass to Jack. “You’re the only man in California who knows what that cost.”
And Jack, whose team has just lost a football game on the last play, laughs until his eyes water.
Lena has been watching him laugh. “You look like something happened to you.”
“Ohio State beat Michigan.”
“That was *yesterday*.”
“It’s still happening to me.”
She narrows her eyes at him. Then Julian asks her about a yellow flag on the big screen, and she turns to answer him.

With four minutes left the Bucs are throwing on every down, and the Saints send an extra defensive back trotting onto the field, and Julian, who has been told twice, leans across Lena’s chair. “Sorry. The nickel,” he says to Jack. “What is it, again?”

journal.title: Dale (Sully’s)
journal.text: Dale Wisniewski. Warren, Michigan — not the other one. Twenty-seven years at Warren Truck, laid off in the spring. Barry Sanders jersey; tips in quarters. He knows about Dad now. She says the Lions are the Aints of the North and he’s welcome in the booth. Lions 38, Browns 37, on the last play. He bought me a root beer: the only man in California who knows what that cost.

journal.title: Dale (Sully’s)
journal.text: Dale Wisniewski. A Lions fan alone at the end of Sully’s bar in a Barry Sanders jersey. Warren, Michigan — not the other one. Tips in quarters. Said the rookie’s going to be good. Lions 38, Browns 37, on the last play. He bought me a root beer: the only man in California who knows what that cost.

choices.text: “Five DBs. You bring one in when they go three wide.”
response: “Five DBs,” Jack says. “You bring one in when they go three wide.” And then, because that isn’t an explanation, he does it properly, the way his father did it for him in the garage on Glenwood: the ketchup bottle is the quarterback, two coasters are the corners, and his root beer is the fifth defensive back, coming on for a linebacker. Julian gets it on the third try. “Okay. *Okay*,” he says, and thanks him like he means it.
Up on the chair, with the Kleenex at her nose, Lena watches Jack explain football to her boyfriend with a bottle of Heinz.
The clock runs out in Tampa. Thirty-eight to seven. Ten and oh.

response.text: The owner unties the rope for the final, and Lena rings it herself, up on the rung with both hands, until the owner comes down the bar and asks her nicely.
response.else: The owner unties the rope for the final, and Lena rings it, and then holds the end of it out to Jack for the last one.

choices.text: “Ask Lena. She’ll explain it till you cry.”
response: “Ask Lena,” Jack says. “She’ll explain it till you cry.”

She does. The salt shaker is the quarterback, the Kleenex is the slot receiver, and Julian’s car keys, when she gets to them, are the nickel back, sliding over with a jingle to cover. It takes the rest of the drive and most of the voice she has left.
“I’m crying,” Julian says.
“Good,” says Lena. “That’s how you learn.”
The clock runs out in Tampa. Thirty-eight to seven. Ten and oh.

Lena leans down off the chair with her hand flat on the bar and draws the formation on the wood with one finger — three wide out here, the slot, the fifth man coming on over the top to take him — croaking it to Julian a word at a time. Julian follows her finger. Jack watches her draw it.
The clock runs out in Tampa. Thirty-eight to seven. Ten and oh.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 3:10 PM · THE BRICK → DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The third-floor reading room of the Brick makes the sound a hundred people make trying not to make any: radiators ticking under the tall windows, a stapler going somewhere back in the stacks, a page turned carefully, so as not to wake anybody. Outside, the Sunday campus is going home early for the week, roller bags clattering down the path toward the lots. Jack has a long table to himself and a yellow legal pad, and across the top of the first page, in his small square capitals, Hale’s question: WHETHER A PROMISE BINDS WHEN ITS REASON IS GONE. Under it, because Hale assigned it to him: NO.

He argues it for eight pages. A promise is a tool, he writes, made for a job; when the job is gone, the man who goes on keeping it isn’t faithful, he’s only loyal to his own handwriting. Hume says something like it — that the obligation of a promise is an invention, a convention men keep because it pays them — and around four o’clock, with Hume open at his elbow, Jack writes the best paragraph he has written all semester. He doesn’t believe a word of it.
The RAZR lies face down beside the legal pad, where he put it.

choices.text: Leave it face down till Mass.
response: He leaves it there, face down, through Hume and the conclusion and the footnotes.
By half past five it’s dark out. He prints it in the basement, eight pages at a dime a page, and carries it home across the Commons still warm.

At twenty past eight the Fishbowl TV has the American Music Awards on, and Laney is on the couch under it between two of her Pi Lam sisters with a bag of kettle corn. On the screen a girl in a sequined dress stands at a microphone looking astonished to be there; a woman goes by in a headdress made of light.
Laney addresses the television. “Taylor Swift has won everything there is,” she says, “and she’s *still* nicer than me.”
“Everybody’s nicer than you,” one of the sisters says.
“That’s what I *said*.” Laney holds the kettle corn up over the back of the couch without looking, and Jack, on his way through with eight pages and a blazer to find before Mass, takes a handful.
“Mass?” she says, without turning around.
“Nine o’clock.”
“Light a candle for Kanye,” Laney says. “Taylor’s going to be nice to him till he dies.”

He turns it over at half past three. It’s blank. After that he quits counting the times he turns it over. The girl across the table with the flash cards doesn’t; every twenty minutes she looks up at the little click of the hinge.
By half past five it’s dark out. He prints it in the basement, eight pages at a dime a page, and carries it home across the Commons still warm.

s05.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “To Jesus Christ, Our Sovereign King”
body: Christ the King comes in cold. Somebody has propped the doors for the stragglers, and the night off Ocean Road comes up the center aisle to meet the incense halfway. For the last Sunday of the Church’s year the organist has come to the nine o’clock himself, and the guitars are sitting this one out in their cases against the sacristy wall. He takes the entrance hymn at full organ — a hymn written for a cathedral and a thousand voices — and the hundred or so students under the hull of St. Brendan’s do what they can to be a thousand. Father Osei comes up the aisle behind the cross in white and gold, with the little hitch in his step, smiling up at the ceiling like the hymn is a joke he’s been let in on.

Jack has the end of the fourth pew on the right. Lena is beside him in the black mantilla with a roll of cough drops in her lap, and beside her is Julian, in a cardigan, who has most of the responses now. Tonight Lena is down to a whisper, so he says them for the pair of them, a little behind the room, and she mouths along with him. Across the aisle, the fourth pew on the left is full of nursing students.

Kenzie Rourke sings the psalm from the ambo — *The Lord is king; he is robed in majesty* — and on the refrain Lena’s mouth moves and nothing comes out of it but air. Julian, without looking over, sings it a little louder.

The RAZR is on silent in the front pocket of his jeans. Once, during the second reading — *Behold, he is coming amid the clouds* — he feels it go against his leg, and puts his hand over the pocket, and it hasn’t. He keeps his hand there anyway, till the Alleluia.

Father Osei reads the Gospel himself: Pilate in his headquarters, asking a prisoner whether he is a king, and the prisoner answering some other question. *Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.* That’s where it stops.

Osei comes down to the step without notes. “Pilate’s next line, which we did not read tonight, is ‘What is truth?’ — and he asks it with the Truth standing in front of him, close enough to touch. Most of us ask it the same way, my friends, with our backs half turned.” He sits down. Near the back, a baby has a remark to make about that.

body.text: In the quiet after Communion, on the kneeler, he says *Becca* once into his folded hands. A week of it left.

body: Then he gives God what he has: Nonna, still sleeping in the front-room chair so she won’t have to manage the stairs; his father in the garage with the last play of a football game; Gina, who sleeps through first period; Danny, where it’s already midnight. He doesn’t bring up Friday night. He wouldn’t know how to start it, or what he’d be asking for, and he kneels there not knowing until Lena’s elbow tells him it’s time to sit.
The last hymn of the year is the King’s again, the organist pulling out everything he has left, and Lena, who has no voice at all, sings it anyway, an octave under where she means to be, every verse.
